opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so for a long time I was, and in some sense still am, fairly sympathetic to moral realism: the idea that there are facts about what's good that don't depend on any particular agent's preferences. Early on I thought that might make alignment easier. If there's a real target out there, then a sufficiently capable and honest reasoner should converge toward it, the way a good enough scientist converges toward physics.

The obstacle I kept running into was verification. Even if those moral facts exist, I had no way to check, from the outside, whether a given system had actually found them, or whether it had found something that looked like them from where I was standing. With physics you can run an experiment and the world pushes back. With ethics, the "experiments" are things like letting a powerful system act on its conclusions and seeing what happens. By then it's too late if it got it wrong.

So you end up in a strange position. Moral realism might tell you there's a right answer, but it doesn't give you a procedure you can trust for getting there with a system much smarter than you, under adversarial pressure, with very little room for error. "Trust the convergence" isn't an engineering approach. It's a hope.

That's a big part of what pushed me toward something more modest and more formal. Instead of trying to load the whole of ethics into the system and hope it's right, I wanted to specify narrower properties, like safety constraints, bounds on side effects, and limits on what the system is allowed to do in the world. Those are things you can actually write down, model, and in principle prove or at least check with quantified confidence. Maybe a superintelligence could eventually help us with the deep moral questions. But the first step has to be getting to a point where we can safely ask it, and that requires guarantees I couldn't get from realism alone.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually something I thought about pretty seriously for a while. I've long had this intuition that there is something like moral truth out there, that ethics isn't just a matter of taste or convention, that there are facts about what's good that are, in some sense, discoverable. And if you believe that, the tempting move is to say: well, then alignment is easy in principle. Just build a system that's smart enough and honest enough, point it at the moral truth, and it'll converge on the right thing. You don't have to specify human values, you just have to specify "figure out what's actually good and do that."

The obstacle I ran into is that even if moral realism is true, I have no way of verifying that any particular system has actually found the truth rather than something that merely looks like it from the inside. There's no external oracle I can check against. With a mathematical claim, I can demand a proof and check it step by step. With a physical claim, I can run an experiment. But with a moral claim, if the system comes back and says "I've reasoned carefully and the correct thing to do is X," and X is something that strikes me as horrifying, I'm stuck. Either it's right and my intuitions are wrong, or it's gone off the rails and its reasoning is corrupted somewhere I can't see. And from the outside those two cases look identical.

So the problem isn't metaphysical, it's epistemic. Moral realism, even if true, doesn't give you a verification procedure. And alignment, as an engineering discipline, is fundamentally about verification. It's about being able to say, with justified confidence, that this system will behave within certain bounds before you deploy it. If the only check is "the system says it's being good," you've just reinvented the problem.

That's a big part of why I ended up moving toward approaches where the guarantees are about things I actually can verify: formal specifications, bounded behaviors, world models you can inspect. You scale back the ambition from "make it do the right thing" to "make it provably not do certain catastrophic things, and keep humans in the loop for the rest." It's less philosophically satisfying, but it's something you can actually build on.

astra-6.text: The obstacle was that moral realism doesn’t, by itself, give you a procedure for discovering moral truth. Even if I believe there are objectively right answers to moral questions, I still have to explain how an AI could reliably find them—and how we could tell that it had, rather than merely becoming very confident in some mistaken moral theory. So there’s a gap between that philosophical belief and an actionable approach to alignment.

sol-6.1.text: The obstacle was that believing there are objective moral truths doesn’t give you a procedure for finding them. Even if there’s a right answer to what we ought to do, how do you specify a computational process that reliably discovers it? And how do you know that process is tracking moral truth rather than just reproducing your own intuitions? I couldn’t bridge that gap well enough to make moral realism itself into a concrete alignment proposal.
